description: We are Team IBÑ Drop Table, five computer science students from Zaragoza, Spain. For the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge we built Eskai, a public web tool to watch the infrared sky change with real SPHEREx data. We believe tools for exploring space should be clear, honest about their limits, and open to everyone, from students to citizen scientists. More about us and our work: our GitHub organization.
summary:
Eskai is a public web tool that lets anyone watch the infrared sky change using real NASA SPHEREx data. Type the RA/Dec of a patch of sky, or point at the sky from where you stand, and flick through every SPHEREx visit to that spot like an astronomer's blink comparator, the method that found Pluto in 1930. A difference layer subtracts one visit from another so moving objects stand out in red and blue, and a game teaches people to spot them, with answers checked against proper motions measured by ESA's Gaia. The five challenge objects open instantly; any other position is processed live in about a minute.

Eskai is built to be trusted. Saturated objects, contaminated pixels and weak signals are flagged on screen, and automatic detections are labelled as beta candidates for people to verify. SPHEREx will return more data than any team can sift through alone. Eskai gives many people a clear, honest way to help look for the next moving object.
details:
Eskai: look up
In 1930, Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto by flicking between two photographic plates and spotting the one dot that moved. Today, NASA's SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months in 102 infrared bands, with images of more than a billion objects. No one can search all of it alone. Eskai puts Tombaugh's method in anyone's hands, with real 2026 data, and makes it clear what the data can and cannot show.

WHAT A VISITOR CAN DO
1. Choose a patch of sky
- Type RA/Dec in decimal degrees or sexagesimal (e.g. 08h55m10s, -7d14m42s) and a field of view, or move the all-sky map and press "See SPHEREx data for this spot".
- Point at the sky ("What is above you?"): on a computer, enter your location (or let the browser share it) and set direction and height with two sliders; on a phone, the compass and tilt sensors can do the aiming (marked approximate). The map shows that part of the sky right now and suggests the nearest of the five challenge objects. Location and orientation never leave the device.
- Points of interest: the five challenge objects, each one tap away.

2. Watch it change
- One SPHEREx image per visit, with play, pause, step and a speed menu (1 to 24 frames per second). Every frame uses the same contrast, so what changes is real.
- The sky around the patch: the SPHEREx patch sits in its exact place on NASA's WISE infrared sky (AllWISE), and you can drag and zoom the sky around it while the patch stays glued to its position. Hide the SPHEREx picture to see only its outline over the WISE sky, or hide the surroundings to look at SPHEREx alone. A label always says which part is SPHEREx and which is WISE.

- Difference layer: subtracts one visit from another (consecutive visits, or first versus last). What stays put disappears; what moves shows up red (brighter later) or blue (brighter earlier).
- Rings and an arrow mark where a known mover should be, from its catalogued proper motion.
- Detections (beta): software flags candidates on the first-versus-last difference, coloured by kind (appeared, disappeared, contaminated) and labelled as needing human verification.

3. See what infrared reveals
- H2O, CO2 and CO filter layers.
- A spectrum chart coloured by detector (6 detectors, up to 102 channels), with molecular windows shaded. In Epsilon Indi B, the methane signature is visible.
- Click any point of the image to see the spectrum of that spot. Live spectra are sparse (about one channel per detector) and are labelled as such.
- Light curve: brightness at every visit, with error bars.
- Eye vs infrared: a draggable bar compares visible light (DSS2) with infrared (AllWISE).

4. Learn and take part
- Find what moves (game): 3 to 5 rounds on Barnard's Star and Epsilon Indi B. Two real visits flicker; click where something moved. The server scores each guess against Gaia DR3 proper motions, then shows the object's real path. Rounds where the motion is under one pixel say so and offer a hint. Players end with a leaderboard and a shareable "Star hunter" card marked "A game score, not a discovery".
- Citizen sightings: pick a point, say what you think it is (asteroid, brown dwarf, high proper-motion star, variable star, transient), and others can confirm it with "I see it too". Every report creates a share card with the SPHEREx cutout, coordinates and the label "Unverified candidate: needs human confirmation".
- Ask about it: an assistant explains what is on screen in an Easy or Technical style, together with the object's caveats. "What is catalogued here?" lists SIMBAD objects within 2 arcmin without AI, so nothing can be invented.

5. Share it
- Every view is a link (?ra=&dec=&fov=&band=&view=), so any finding can be shared or reopened exactly.

HOW ESKAI ANSWERS THE CHALLENGE
- Enter RA/Dec of a patch of sky: yes, in two formats, plus map and sky pointing.
- Show the images like a little video: yes, a player over every SPHEREx visit.
- Test on the five objects: Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis are all precomputed and open instantly, each with its own scientific note.
- Subtract images taken at different times: Difference layer, consecutive and first versus last.
- Display the 102 bands creatively, with spectra on the fly: molecule layers, detector-coloured spectra, click-for-spectrum anywhere.
- Field of view: 1 to 15 arcmin for any place processed live.
- Overlay other telescopes: NASA's WISE infrared all-sky survey (AllWISE) as the sky map and in the eye-vs-infrared comparison; Gaia DR3 proper motions predict where each known mover should be.
- Query through the URL: every view is a link.
- Metadata such as contamination flags: shown on detections and in caveats.
- Public tools: Aladin Lite (CDS) and SIMBAD.
- Easy to update with new releases: the viewer hard-codes no images or visits; the backend is regenerated with a script.

VALIDATED ON THE FIVE CHALLENGE OBJECTS
- Each object has 3 to 4 SPHEREx visits between April 2025 and September 2026.
- Barnard's Star moves 10.3 arcsec between the first and last visit, against 10.2 arcsec expected from Gaia.
- Game answers match the images within 0.7 pixels.
- WISE 0855: at 4.4 to 5 microns, the brightest pixel falls within one pixel of the predicted position in 79% of 43 images. The signal per image is weak (median S/N 3.8), so we report it as faintly visible, not detected.
- Barnard's Star and R Draconis saturate the detector. Eskai says so instead of showing an invented spectrum.
- The sky-pointing maths (direction, place and time to RA/Dec) was checked against astropy on 40 random cases: worst error 27 arcsec.

HONEST BY DESIGN
Each object card carries its scientific caveat in one line, with "why?" for the full note. When the archive does not answer, Eskai shows cached data and a banner says it belongs to another position. The assistant always says "AI assistant: it can be wrong. Findings need human verification." We never claim a discovery: users make sightings of candidates, and people decide.

WHO IT HELPS
- The public and students: start from the sky above them and learn how astronomers really find moving objects.
- Citizen scientists: a guided, trustworthy way into SPHEREx data, in the spirit of projects like Backyard Worlds, where volunteers have found most known brown dwarfs.
- Researchers and educators: share or embed an exact view with a link.

HOW IT IS BUILT
- Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS 4, Recharts and Aladin Lite 3, with self-hosted fonts. Works on computers and phones (bottom tab bar, 44 px touch targets); keyboard accessible; animations stop for users who ask for reduced motion.
- Backend: Python / FastAPI, hosted on Render. It fetches SPHEREx cutouts from NASA/IPAC IRSA, builds per-visit and difference images, corrects positions for proper motion with Gaia DR3, and queries SIMBAD with caching and fallbacks.
- Resilience: if the server is waking up, the archive is slow, or a service is down, the visitor sees what is happening and gets cached data with a clear notice, never a blank screen. The landing page needs no backend at all.

CREATIVITY
Eskai turns a 1930 discovery technique into a game and a citizen-science tool. It lets people start from the sky above them, see what their eyes miss in infrared, and learn to tell what moves from what doesn't, and why some data can't be trusted.

NEXT STEPS
Automatic updates with each SPHEREx release, larger fields of view to follow faster-moving objects, co-adding images to improve signal-to-noise, and game rounds with WISE 0855.
